entry:
Historical region and cultural area of central and southern [[Mexico]] and northern Central America, home to indigenous civilizations before the Spanish conquest. It comprises central and southern Mexico, all of Belize, Guatemala, El Salvador, western Honduras, and the Greater Nicoya region of Nicaragua and Costa Rica, and is defined by a mosaic of cultural traits shared among its peoples. Societies flourished there for more than 3,000 years before [[Spanish colonization of the Americas]] began on Hispaniola in 1493. It is one of six regions where ancient civilizations arose independently (see [[Cradle of civilization]]) and one of five where writing developed independently.

Beginning as early as 7000 BCE, the domestication of cacao, [[Maize|maize]], beans, tomato, avocado, vanilla, squash, and chili, along with the turkey and dog, led hunter-gatherers to settle in agricultural villages. Shared traits included a complex mythological and religious tradition, a vigesimal numeric system, a complex calendar, ball playing, and a distinct architectural style. Ceremonial centers were linked by trade in obsidian, jade, cacao, cinnabar, hematite, and ceramics. Mesoamericans knew of the wheel and basic metallurgy, but neither became technologically relevant.

The Olmec of the Gulf Coast were among the earliest complex civilizations. In the preclassic period urban polities arose among the Maya, at centers such as Calakmul, El Mirador, and [[Tikal]], and among the Zapotec at Monte Albán. The first true writing systems appeared among the Epi-Olmec and Zapotec and reached their height in Classic Maya script. [[Teotihuacan]] built a military and commercial empire and collapsed around 600 CE. The Toltec later dominated central Mexico, and the [[Aztecs]] built a tributary empire covering most of central Mesoamerica.

The Spanish conquest in the 16th century ended the distinct tradition. Eurasian diseases such as [[Smallpox|smallpox]] and measles caused the deaths of upwards of 90% of the indigenous people. Many of their descendants still speak ancestral languages.

Historical region of West Asia within the [[Tigris]]–[[Euphrates]] river system, in the northern part of the [[Fertile Crescent]], corresponding roughly to modern [[Iraq]]. The name is Greek for "[land] between rivers." In the broader sense the region also includes parts of present-day Iran, Turkey, Syria, and Kuwait. A distinction is usually made between Upper Mesopotamia, from the rivers' sources down to [[Baghdad]], and Lower Mesopotamia, from Baghdad to the [[Persian Gulf]].

Mesopotamia is the site of the earliest developments of the [[Neolithic Revolution]] from around 10,000 BC and is recognized as the cradle of some of the world's earliest civilizations. It has been credited with inspiring the invention of the [[Wheel|wheel]], the planting of the first cereal crops, cursive script, mathematics, astronomy, and agriculture. Fertile alluvial plains and irrigation supported early city-states such as [[Uruk]]. Sumerians, said to have invented [[Cuneiform|cuneiform]] writing around 3100 BC, and Akkadians dominated the region from the beginning of recorded history (c. 3100 BC) to the fall of Babylon in 539 BC.

Empires began with [[Sargon of Akkad]] around 2350 BC. In the early second millennium BC, society polarized into [[Assyria]] in the north and [[Babylonia]] in the south. The [[Neo-Assyrian Empire]] controlled much of the ancient Near East from 900 to 612 BC. The Babylonians then dominated for a century as the last independent Mesopotamian realm until the modern era. Cyrus the Great's Achaemenid Empire conquered the region in 539 BC, and [[Alexander the Great]] in 332 BC. After Alexander's death the Seleucids prevailed over the other successors. Around 150 BC the [[Parthian Empire]] held Mesopotamia, which became a battleground between Romans and Parthians. In 226 AD the eastern regions fell to the Sassanid Persians under Ardashir I. The division between the Roman and Sasanian empires lasted until the 7th century Muslim conquest.

After the Islamic conquest the region came to be known as Iraq; Upper Mesopotamia became al-Jazira and Lower Mesopotamia al-Sawad.

Set of life-sustaining chemical reactions occurring within living organisms. The word comes from the Greek *metabolē*, "change." Its three main functions are converting the energy in food into a form usable for cellular processes, converting food into building blocks of macromolecules such as proteins, lipids, [[Nucleic acid|nucleic acids]], and some carbohydrates, and excreting metabolic wastes. These enzyme-catalyzed reactions allow organisms to grow, reproduce, maintain their structures, and respond to their environments.

Reactions are classed as catabolic, the breaking down of compounds (for example, of [[Glucose|glucose]] to pyruvate by [[Cellular respiration|cellular respiration]]), or anabolic, the building up of compounds by biosynthesis. Usually catabolism releases energy and anabolism consumes it. Catabolism supplies [[Adenosine triphosphate|adenosine triphosphate]] (ATP), the primary energy currency, produced through pathways such as [[Glycolysis|glycolysis]] and, under aerobic conditions, mainly in the mitochondria through the [[Citric acid cycle|citric acid cycle]] and oxidative phosphorylation.

Reactions are organized into metabolic pathways, in which one chemical is transformed through a series of steps, each facilitated by a specific [[Enzyme|enzyme]]. Enzymes allow organisms to drive reactions that require energy by coupling them to spontaneous reactions that release energy, and they allow the rate of a reaction to be regulated in response to the cell's environment or signals from other cells.

An organism's metabolic system determines which substances it finds nutritious and which poisonous: some [[Prokaryote|prokaryotes]] use hydrogen sulfide (H₂S) as a nutrient, yet the gas is poisonous to some animals. The basal metabolic rate measures the energy consumed by all these reactions at rest. Basic pathways are strikingly similar across vastly different species; the carboxylic acids of the citric acid cycle occur in all known organisms, from *Escherichia coli* to elephants, which probably reflects their early appearance in evolution. Normal metabolism is disrupted in diseases such as type II diabetes, metabolic syndrome, and [[Cancer|cancer]], whose cells metabolize differently from normal cells, a difference that can help identify therapeutic targets.

Material that, when polished or fractured, shows a lustrous appearance and conducts electricity and heat relatively well. The English word derives from Ancient Greek *métallon*, "mine, quarry, metal." These properties are associated with having electrons available at the Fermi level, as opposed to nonmetallic materials, which do not. Metals are typically ductile, able to be drawn into a wire, and malleable, able to be shaped by hammering or pressing.

A metal may be a [[Chemical element|chemical element]], such as [[Iron|iron]], an [[Alloy|alloy]], such as [[Stainless steel|stainless steel]], or a molecular compound, such as polymeric sulfur nitride. The general science of metals is [[Metallurgy|metallurgy]], a subtopic of [[Materials science|materials science]]; their electronic and thermal properties also fall within [[Condensed matter physics|condensed matter physics]] and solid-state chemistry. In everyday use, steel alloys are called metals, while polymers, wood, and ceramics are nonmetallic. Many elements and compounds become metallic under high pressure; iodine gradually becomes a metal at a pressure between 40 and 170 thousand times atmospheric.

Most metals are shiny, at least when polished or fractured. Densities vary widely: [[Lithium|lithium]] is the least dense of the elemental metals (0.534 g/cm³) and [[Osmium|osmium]] the most dense (22.59 g/cm³). Magnesium, aluminium, and titanium are light metals of commercial importance, with densities of 1.7, 2.7, and 4.5 g/cm³, compared with 7.9 for iron and 8.9 for copper. Metals typically deform under stress without cleaving, and their reversible elastic deformation is described well by [[Hooke's law]]. The atoms of simple metals are often in one of three crystal structures: body-centered cubic, face-centered cubic, or hexagonal close-packed.

Metals conduct electricity because, when a voltage is applied, some electrons shift to slightly higher-momentum states, which are available at energies near the highest occupied levels; by the [[Pauli exclusion principle]], no two electrons can occupy the same quantum state. Semiconductors such as [[Silicon|silicon]] instead have an energy gap between filled and empty states. The elemental metals have electrical conductivities from 6.9 × 10³ S/cm for manganese to 6.3 × 10⁵ S/cm for silver, and conductivity usually decreases with heating. All metallic alloys, as well as conducting ceramics and polymers, are metals by the same definition, as are liquids such as [[Mercury (element)|mercury]].

The strength and resilience of some metals have led to frequent use in high-rise building and bridge construction, most vehicles, many home appliances, tools, pipes, and railroad tracks. Precious metals were historically used as coinage, and coinage metals have now extended to at least 23 of the chemical elements. The history of refined metals is thought to begin with the use of copper about 11,000 years ago. Gold, silver, iron (as meteoric iron), lead, and brass were likewise in use before the first known appearance of bronze in the fifth millennium BCE. Sodium, the first light metal, was discovered in 1809, and since the end of World War II more sophisticated alloys have been developed.

Domain of [[Materials science|materials science]] and engineering that studies the physical and chemical behavior of metallic elements, their intermetallic compounds, and their mixtures, known as [[Alloy|alloys]]. It covers both the science and the technology of metals, including their production and the engineering of metal components. It is distinct from the craft of [[Metalworking|metalworking]] in providing a scientific foundation for it, much as medical science supports the practice of medicine. The word derives from Ancient Greek *metallourgós*, "worker in metal," and was originally an alchemist's term for extracting metals from minerals.

The science divides into chemical metallurgy and physical metallurgy. Chemical metallurgy is chiefly concerned with the reduction and oxidation of metals and their chemical performance, including mineral processing, extraction, [[Thermodynamics|thermodynamics]], [[Electrochemistry|electrochemistry]], and corrosion. Physical metallurgy focuses on mechanical and physical properties and performance, including [[Crystallography|crystallography]], material characterization, phase transformations, and failure mechanisms. The study of metal production is subdivided into ferrous metallurgy, based on iron, and non-ferrous metallurgy, based on other metals; ferrous production accounts for 95% of world metal production. Traditional areas include mineral processing, heat treatment, failure analysis, and joining by welding, brazing, and soldering; emerging areas include [[Nanotechnology|nanotechnology]], superconductors, composites, biomedical materials, and surface engineering.

The earliest metal employed by humans appears to be gold, which occurs native; small amounts of natural gold dating to the late Paleolithic, 40,000 BCE, have been found in Spanish caves. Early cold metallurgy using native copper is documented in Anatolia and at Tell Maghzaliyah in Iraq, from the 7th to 6th millennia BCE. The earliest evidence of [[Smelting|smelting]] in Eurasia comes from the Balkans and Carpathian Mountains, with objects dated to around 6,200 to 5,000 BCE; copper smelting in the 6th millennium BCE has been found in present-day Serbia, and a smelted copper axe from Pločnik dates to 5,500 BCE. The earliest documented use of lead in the Near East dates from the 6th millennium BCE. Copper smelting is documented in Anatolia and southeastern Iran from c. 5,000 BCE and in northern Egypt from c. 4,000 BCE.

Branch of [[Philosophy|philosophy]] that examines the basic nature or most fundamental structure of reality. It is traditionally seen as the study of mind-independent features of the world, though some theorists view it as an inquiry into the conceptual framework of human understanding. Some philosophers, including [[Aristotle]], call it "first philosophy," suggesting that it is more fundamental than other forms of philosophical inquiry. It is one of the oldest branches of philosophy, and its precise nature is disputed.

Its topics include existence, the features all entities share and their division into categories of being, objects and their properties, possibility and necessity, space, time, and change, causation and the laws of nature, the relation of mind and matter, and whether everything is predetermined or there is [[Free will|free will]]. An influential division is between particulars, unique individual entities such as a specific apple, and universals, general features such as the color red. Metaphysics differs from the individual sciences, which examine more specific and concrete features of particular classes of entities; the extent to which this contrast is strict is disputed.

Two historically influential definitions understand metaphysics as the science of first causes and as the study of being as being. Starting with [[Immanuel Kant]], an alternative conception focused on conceptual schemes rather than external reality. P. F. Strawson later contrasted descriptive metaphysics, which articulates the schemes commonly used to understand the world, with revisionary metaphysics, which aims to produce better ones. Metaphysicians typically rely on rational intuitions and abstract reasoning but also use empirical approaches linked to scientific theories. Critics question the reliability of its methods and the meaningfulness of its theories.

The name comes from the Greek *ta meta ta phusika*, "what comes after the physics." It may refer to topics lying beyond [[Physics|physics]], or may stem from an editor, likely Andronicus of Rhodes, placing Aristotle's treatise on the subject after his works on physics. Its roots lie in speculation about the origin of the universe in the Upanishads of ancient India, Taoism in ancient China, and pre-Socratic philosophy in ancient Greece. Medieval Western discussion of universals was shaped by [[Plato]] and Aristotle, and the modern period produced comprehensive systems, many of them idealist. In the 20th century, traditional metaphysics and idealism in particular faced criticism that prompted new approaches.

Country in North America (pop., 2025: c. 131 million), officially the United Mexican States, with its capital at [[Mexico City]]. It is the northernmost country in Latin America, bordering the United States to the north and Guatemala and Belize to the southeast, with coasts on the Pacific Ocean, the Caribbean Sea, and the Gulf of Mexico. It covers 1,972,550 sq km and has the world's largest number of native Spanish speakers.

Human presence dates back to at least 11,500 BC. [[Mesoamerica]] was home to societies including the Olmecs, Maya, Zapotecs, Teotihuacan civilization, and Purépecha. Spanish colonization began in 1521, when an indigenous alliance defeated the [[Aztec Empire]], establishing the colony of [[New Spain]] with its capital at Tenochtitlan, now Mexico City. Silver mining and its position as a hub between Europe and Asia made it a major center of the transoceanic economy. The 1810–1821 [[Mexican War of Independence]] ended Spanish rule. In 1848 Mexico lost nearly half its territory in the [[Mexican–American War]]. The Constitution of 1857 led to civil war and French intervention, and the Second Mexican Empire under Maximilian I was overthrown by Republican forces led by [[Benito Juárez]]. The long dictatorship of [[Porfirio Díaz]] was ended by the 1910–1920 [[Mexican Revolution]], which produced the 1917 Constitution. Industrialization and growth in the 1940s–1970s were accompanied by electoral fraud and economic crises, and the North American Free Trade Agreement took effect in 1994.

Mexico is a federal republic with a presidential system and a separation of powers into executive, legislative, and judicial branches. The bicameral Congress of the Union comprises the Chamber of Deputies and the Senate, and the country has 32 states.

It is a newly industrialized and developing country with the world's 13th-largest economy by nominal GDP and by purchasing power parity. It ranks first in the Americas and seventh in the world by number of UNESCO World Heritage Sites, and is one of 17 megadiverse countries. It received 42.2 million international arrivals in 2022. Poverty, corruption, and crime remain widespread; since 2006, approximately 127,000 deaths have been attributed to conflict between drug trafficking syndicates. Mexico belongs to the United Nations, the G20, the OECD, the World Trade Organization, and APEC.

Capital and largest city of [[Mexico]] (pop., 2020: 9,209,944; Greater Mexico City 21,804,515), the most populous city in North America. Located in the Valley of Mexico on the high Mexican Central Plateau, it sits at an altitude of 2,240 m and is divided into 16 boroughs, or *alcaldías*, which are subdivided into neighborhoods, or *colonias*. The city proper has a land area of 1,495 sq km and is the second-largest Spanish-speaking city proper in the world after [[Lima]]. Greater Mexico City is the world's 15th-largest metropolitan area and the second-largest urban agglomeration in the Western Hemisphere after [[São Paulo]]. In 2011 it had a GDP of $411 billion and accounted for about 22% of Mexico's GDP; the city itself accounted for 15.8%.

It is the oldest capital city in the Americas and one of only two founded by Indigenous peoples. It began as [[Tenochtitlan]], a Mexica city built around 1325 on islands in Lake Texcoco. After the 1521 siege it was nearly destroyed and rebuilt to Spanish urban standards. The municipality was established as México Tenochtitlán in 1524 and has been officially called Ciudad de México since 1585. During the colonial period it was a major political, administrative, and financial center, the capital of [[New Spain]]. After independence, the surrounding territory was organized in 1824 as the country's only federal district, the Distrito Federal. Baron [[Alexander von Humboldt]] is credited with the nickname City of Palaces.

Residents won the right to elect the head of government and the unicameral Legislative Assembly in 1997, and since then the Party of the Democratic Revolution and later Morena, both left-wing, have controlled both offices. The city has adopted policies including legal abortion, no-fault divorce, [[Same-sex marriage|same-sex marriage]], and legal gender change. On January 29, 2016, the Federal District was officially renamed Ciudad de México, or CDMX. A constitutional clause still prevents it from becoming a state while it remains the capital.

Its informal demonym is *chilango*; residents are formally called *capitalinos*. Sources also note land subsidence of more than 40 cm a year in some zones from groundwater extraction, vulnerability to earthquakes on soft lakebed soils, and air pollution from vehicles and industry.

English chemist and physicist who contributed vastly to electrochemistry and [[Electromagnetism|electromagnetism]]. He received little formal education and became, as an autodidact, one of the most influential scientists in history. He was born in Newington Butts, [[Surrey]], to a poor family; at 14 he became an apprentice to a bookbinder and bookseller, and during his seven-year apprenticeship he read widely and attended lectures. In 1812 he heard lectures by [[Humphry Davy]], sent Davy a 300-page book based on his notes, and in 1813 was appointed Chemical Assistant at the Royal Institution. He later became its first Fullerian Professor of Chemistry, a lifetime position.

His research on the magnetic field around a conductor carrying a [[Direct current|direct current]] established the concept of the [[Electromagnetic field|electromagnetic field]] in physics. He discovered the principles of [[Electromagnetic induction|electromagnetic induction]], diamagnetism, and the laws of [[Electrolysis|electrolysis]]. His inventions of electromagnetic rotary devices formed the foundation of [[Electric motor|electric motor]] technology, and it was largely due to his efforts that electricity became practical for use in technology. He also established that magnetism could affect rays of light. As a chemist he discovered [[Benzene|benzene]] and tetrachloroethylene, invented an early form of the Bunsen burner and the system of oxidation numbers, and popularised terms such as "anode," "cathode," "electrode," and "ion."

He was an experimentalist who conveyed his ideas in clear, simple language and thought in a visual manner; his mathematics did not extend beyond the simplest algebra. [[James Clerk Maxwell]] summarized his work and that of others in equations accepted as the basis of all modern theories of electromagnetic phenomena. He devoted considerable effort to public service, working on lighthouses and protecting ships from corrosion, and with [[Charles Lyell]] investigated a colliery explosion at Haswell, showing for the first time that coal dust contributed to its severity. He refused to work on chemical weapons for the Crimean War, citing ethical reservations. He founded the Royal Institution's Friday Evening Discourses and popularized its Christmas Lecture Series. The SI unit of capacitance, the farad, is named after him.

American singer, songwriter, dancer, and philanthropist, called the "King of Pop." Born in Gary, Indiana, the eighth of ten children in the Jackson family, he made his public debut at age six as lead singer of [[The Jackson 5]], which signed with [[Motown]]. He rose to solo stardom with *[[Off the Wall]]* (1979) and achieved global success with *[[Thriller (album)|Thriller]]* (1982), which became the best-selling album in history. The music videos for "Thriller," "Beat It," and "Billie Jean" are credited with redefining the medium, and he popularized dance moves such as the moonwalk, the robot, and the anti-gravity lean.

*[[Bad (album)|Bad]]* (1987) was the first album to produce five U.S. Billboard Hot 100 number-one singles. *Dangerous* (1991), *HIStory* (1995), and *Invincible* (2001) followed. He scored 13 number-one singles on the Billboard Hot 100 and is the only artist with a U.S. top-ten single in six decades. His estimated worldwide solo sales exceed 500 million records, and he is one of three musicians, with [[Paul McCartney]] and [[Phil Collins]], to have sold more than 100 million records both as a solo artist and as a principal member of a band. His honors include 13 [[Grammy Awards|Grammy Awards]], 26 American Music Awards, 8 MTV Video Music Awards, and two inductions into the [[Rock and Roll Hall of Fame]]. He donated an estimated $500 million to charity.

From the mid-1980s he came under public scrutiny for his relationships, lifestyle, and changing appearance. He was accused of child sexual abuse in 1993 and settled a civil case out of court in 1994, without admission of guilt. In 2005 he was tried and acquitted on other child sexual abuse charges. The 2019 documentary *Leaving Neverland* detailed further allegations against him.

While preparing for *This Is It*, a series of comeback concerts, he died in 2009 from acute propofol intoxication; his personal physician, Conrad Murray, was held responsible for negligent administration, and the death was ruled a homicide. His death caused unprecedented surges in internet traffic and a spike in music sales. Posthumous releases include the documentary *Michael Jackson's This Is It* (2009) and the albums *Michael* (2010) and *Xscape* (2014).
